title: Score
description: One product's three-axis score, as sources/scores/<slug>.yaml, one file per product (472 of them on 2026-08-08). The file records a judgment AND the evidence for it: what the score is, what it was read off, which sources say so, when they were read, and when the whole axis was last confirmed. Written by a curator or a scoring agent, plus build/apply_scores.py, which may write openness.score and openness.class and nothing else. Read by build/validate.py and the gates beside it, by build/serialize.py into build/notebook_data.json (the payload the notebooks and the front end consume), and by build/serialize_rubric.py into the warehouse. docs/methodology.md is the reader-facing account of the three axes; docs/reference/openness.md, evidence-and-freshness.md and evidence-and-freshness.md are normative on openness, on dates, and on how a date is earned.

product.description: The slug of the product this file scores, and it must equal the filename stem. Every join in the pipeline keys on the stem - sources/products/<slug>.yaml, the category roster, the org roster - so build/validate.py rejects a file whose inner value disagrees: a copied or renamed file with a stale inner name passes every other check and then makes one record reachable under two names. Called `product` rather than `name` because a score is about a product rather than being one. The slug is the product's identity and the key deep links are built on, so it names the tier the vendor sells rather than a version or a size, and it may only be retired by being recorded as an alias on the product that replaced it, which validate.py also enforces. See docs/reference/identity.md.

openness.description:
How open the product is: the axis with a ladder, a recorded evidence string and the most gates.

The three axes are one shape under three sets of names, given at three different times. A reader who learns one should recognize the next:

  concept          openness       adoption       capability
  ---------------  -------------  -------------  ---------------------
  graded judgment  score          level          score
  vocabulary       class          (reach)*       -
  instrument       the ladder*    signal_type    basis, basis_detail
  recorded inputs  components     -              relative_to, relation
  evidence         sources        sources        sources
  confirmation     last_verified  last_verified  last_verified

* Openness's instrument is the category's `scoring_recipe`, which is a category-level declaration rather than a field on the score. Adoption's `reach` is derived from `level` in build/serialize.py and deliberately not stored.

Openness is the only axis whose judgment is reproducible from what this file records: the recipe walks `components` and emits the (score, class) pair, and build/check_rubric.py replays it. docs/reference/openness.md is normative.

score.description: The graded openness judgment, 0-5, and half of what a ladder emits; `class` is the other half and the two are written together. Graded relative to what is achievable WITHIN a product type, so a model at 2 and a deployment tool at 2 are not comparable and `class` is the field to position a product on a spectrum with; docs/reference/openness.md is normative on that and on what each rung means per ladder. Hand-assigned for most of the corpus, and written by build/apply_scores.py where the category's recipe computes it - that tool writes this and `class` and nothing else, and is loud when the computed value differs. Null is an abstention, and a non-null score needs at least one source (build/validate.py); no product abstains today, all 472 openness axes are scored (2026-08-08). Read by check_verification's producible-pair gate, which requires (score, class) to be an outcome some rule in the recipe can actually emit: 17 pairs were not, `4 / open_source` among them, since no software rule pairs 4 with that class (4 is `open_core`).

class.description: The openness VOCABULARY: the band a reader sees, paired with `score`. Eleven values, one per rung any ladder can emit — the software, model, dataset and hardware ladders do not share a vocabulary, which is why this is longer than the five a single ladder uses. `docs/openness-class-map.json` maps each to a display label, a gradient and the three-way open / open-ish / closed bucket the payload carries. Until 2026-08-08 this was an unconstrained string and the vocabulary lived only in that map and in build/render.py.

components.description: The evidence the openness score was read off, as an entry per dimension the category's ladder asks about: a structured mapping, `key -> {value, detail?, raw?}`, plus a reserved `free_text` list for keyless clauses. `value` is the bare token a rule reads, `detail` is the parenthetical or trailing prose a human reads but no formula sees, and `raw` carries the original clause verbatim for the entries whose `{value, detail}` split cannot reproduce it byte-for-byte. A LICENSE key takes the second shape instead - a LIST of `{name, detail?, raw?}` parts, one per license the product makes you accept - because a product can be governed by more than one and `license_tier` resolves every part with the most restrictive governing. The list is what the curator recorded, so nothing infers the part count from a `+` at read time: `culturax`'s `follows mC4 + OSCAR-2301 terms` is ONE part because it is one declared name, and the pre-structured reader needed a whole-string pre-check ahead of its splitter to get that right. Any key whose name contains `license` takes the list (five in the corpus; three are named in some ladder's `license_tier.reads`). This is the most load-bearing field in the corpus, because a category is ladderable only if its VALUES are controlled tokens some dimension's declared enum contains - `edge_hardware` is 71% prose by check_rubric's measure and cannot be laddered whatever its recipe says. Written by whoever scores the product, and edited in place ONLY through build/components.py, which locates the field by indent and re-emits it through the YAML dumper rather than by regex, because a folded scalar spliced by a line-oriented substitution corrupts silently. Read by build/check_rubric.py (replays the formula against it), check_verification (the dimensions recorded here are the invariant's scope), check_parity.py (the repo/warehouse differential), and serialize_rubric.py, which emits one warehouse evidence row per component and warns on a key no dimension declares or `reads` - such a key is dropped from the score silently, which is this corpus's recurring bug. Every reader goes through build.check_rubric.components_of, which returns the same key -> clause dict; nothing in the repo should call split_components directly on this field. build/check_components.py asserts the mapping is the only shape this field may take - a string here fails the gate rather than being skipped, which is what closed the migration. Measured 2026-08-11: on all 472 files, 137 distinct keys, of which each ladder declares a handful (`license` on 439, `source` on 298, `core-gated` on 164).

governing_release.description: For a product whose slug covers a tier rather than a release, which release this openness score describes. The combine rule is that the CURRENT release governs, resolved most-restrictive across that release's distributed SKUs, so the score is about one release even though the slug is about a family - and without this the reader cannot tell which. Adoption and capability combine differently (max across the tier's releases), which is why this sits on openness alone. Declared, not derived: 6 of the 15 products carrying one are closed or API-only with no artifact to date, so a derivation would cover some and not others and a reader could not tell which kind they were looking at. It is a re-read's job to confirm it still points at the current release - which is why it lives here, inside the axis a last_verified covers, rather than in the identity file it occupied until 2026-08-08 where no freshness mechanism reached it. See docs/reference/identity.md.

confidence.description: How sure the curator was of the openness verdict, on a fixed three-value scale. Hand-written by whoever scored the axis; build/apply_scores.py deliberately never touches it, along with `note` and `sources`, because a tool rewriting human judgment makes its own diffs unreviewable. No gate reads it. Its only consumer is the `Confidence` row in the product detail panel that build/render.py and the notebooks draw. Measured 2026-08-08 it is `high` on 432 of 472 openness axes and `low` on one, so read it as the curator's hedging rather than a calibrated uncertainty. The fields carrying real quality signal are `last_verified` for freshness and the evidence grade in sources/evidence_policy.yaml for whether a source is re-derivable at all.

note.description: Why these components add up to this rung, in a sentence or two of prose. Hand-written, parsed by nothing, rendered as `Why` in the product detail panel. It is the axis's escape valve and therefore its hazard: a judgment recorded only here cannot be checked, refreshed, or noticed when it goes stale. That is exactly what happened on capability, where the peer comparison placing roughly a hundred bands sat in the note until `relative_to` and `relation` pulled it out. So the reasoning belongs here and the facts belong in `components`. Prose in sources/products/<slug>.yaml must not restate what this note and the score already carry; docs/reference/product-copy.md, 'Scored fields', is normative on that.

sources.description: The evidence behind THIS axis, flat and per-axis: a source cited for openness is not evidence for adoption, and the three lists routinely differ. At least one is required for a non-null score (build/validate.py). The flatness is why `establishes` exists - measured 2026-07-30, 324 of 470 openness axes cited a single source asserted to settle weights, data, code and license together, which neither a reader nor a tool can check. For openness these are the LICENSE body, the model or dataset card, the repository, and the pricing page that settles whether a core is gated. This is the axis that can never be fully automated: only `license` and `weights` have a dataset route, so at least one human read is permanent (docs/reference/evidence-and-freshness.md).

last_verified.description: The most recent date on which everything in this axis's score was confirmed still correct. Written when the axis is re-checked against its sources, whether or not the value changed. Absent means never confirmed, in which case freshness falls back to the score file's last commit date. Never backfill it from source access dates: opening a URL is a weaker claim than re-confirming a conclusion, and no aggregation of accessed dates fixes that. Normative definition in docs/reference/evidence-and-freshness.md.

raw.description: The verbatim `openness.components` string this record carried before it was migrated to the structured mapping. The migration is now complete: all 472 score files carry it. It is the reversibility record for the recordings whose `{value, detail}` split cannot be reversed byte-for-byte (1,984 component recordings as of 2026-08-14), the input build/check_components.py compares the mapping against, and the string build/serialize.py puts in the payload so the front end and the rendered notebook see no change from the migration. It is a shadow-phase field and is removed when the mapping becomes the only shape.

adoption.description: How used the product is. The same shape as `openness` under different names: `level` is the graded judgment, `signal_type` is the instrument (openness's ladder, capability's `basis`), and `sources` and `last_verified` mean exactly what they mean on the other two axes. It carries no vocabulary field and no recorded-inputs field: the reader-facing range is derived from `level` in build/serialize.py and emitted as `reach`, and the banding rule lives in docs/methodology.md rather than in a per-category recipe. It is the axis most amenable to automation, because the score IS a banded signal, so re-fetching a download or user count re-derives it.

level.description: The adoption band, 1-5, and the axis's ONLY stored value. The human-readable range (`<10K` … `>10M`) is derived from it in build/serialize.py and emitted as `reach` in the payload, never recorded here: it is the same fact twice, and when it was stored 125 of 417 files contradicted their own level. Null where no usage figure exists to band — a hosted feature of a larger platform, or an internal eval suite. Null is an abstention, not a gap.

reach.description: The band's human-readable label, and the UNIT it was read in. Not `level` restated: 20k stars and 20k downloads are not the same reach, so the same level maps to different labels depending on what was counted. The scale is a property of the product TYPE - software and model band package and hub downloads (`<10K` … `>10M`), dataset bands two orders lower (`<1k` … `>1M`) because fetching a corpus is rarer than installing a package, and hardware is qualitative (`niche` / `broad` / `mass-market`) because units shipped are not countable from an artifact. `sources/categories/base_pretrained.yaml` is the only category that declares its bands today, under `scoring_recipe.adoption.bands`; the other fifteen follow a convention that exists nowhere but in the agreement of their own files. Measured 2026-08-08 the corpus holds 34 distinct values, of which roughly eight are real bands and the rest are casing splits (`10k-100k` vs `10K-100K`) and free text (`~14.9k stars`, `50M+ total Docker pulls`) that belongs in `note`.

signal_type.description: WHICH INSTRUMENT the band was read with. Capability's `basis` is the same concept under a different name and a different vocabulary, because the two axes were built at different times; openness's equivalent is the category's ladder, which is why openness carries no such field. `active_users` and `usage_volume` are measured figures, `reported_traction` is a vendor's or a tracker's claim rather than a count, `stars_fallback` is repository popularity standing in for usage, `unknown` is an abstention. The distinction is enforced rather than descriptive: build/validate.py rejects `stars_fallback` above level 3, because stars measure attention rather than use. Measured 2026-08-08: usage_volume 237, reported_traction 108, stars_fallback 84, active_users 23, unknown 20. Also the `Signal` row in the product detail panel.

banded_quantity.description: What the level was actually read off, whenever that is not a current usage figure for this product. Absent means the level is a judgment about the product itself with no borrowed quantity behind it — `claude-opus` and `claude-fable` both record a market-position reading and cite no number at all, which is a real state rather than a gap. Four shapes recur: a parent platform's reach where the product is a feature inside something larger ('Replit platform registered users (50M+, March 2026), not an agent active count'); a real count of the product that is not a current active one (cumulative, all-time, lifetime, or weekly where the scale is written monthly); a proxy of a different kind entirely (revenue, funding, GitHub stars, research citations); and nothing at all, where the note cites a figure only to reject it. Mostly relevant to `reported_traction`, the instrument defined by having no count behind it and the one where the substitution is most common — measured 2026-08-15, 19 of its 109 records band on a parent platform and every one said so in prose a machine could not read. `active_users` had already solved this through the `attribution_note` on its route in sources/signal_routing.yaml; this is that rule given a field. tests/test_banded_quantity.py requires one wherever a `reported_traction` note cites a magnitude, because a number in the prose of an instrument that claims no count is exactly what a reader mistakes for a measurement of the product.

confidence.description: How sure the curator was of the band. Same scale, same author and the same absence of readers as openness.confidence, and worth comparing with it: measured 2026-08-08 adoption is high on 191, medium on 175 and low on 106 of 472, against openness's 432 high. That spread is the honest one, and it reflects how much of the map has no first-party usage figure to band from.

note.description: The prose behind the band: which figure was banded, from where, and what it excludes - 'the OLMo family measured ~14.8M cumulative HF downloads in early 2026; below the Qwen/Llama scale'. Hand-written, read by no tool, rendered as `Detail` in the product detail panel. Where `level` is null this is where the reason for abstaining belongs: 20 products carry no level because no standalone usage figure exists, mostly hosted features of a larger platform (Azure, Bedrock, Vertex, Together) and internal eval suites, and banding those off vendor prose would be inventing the number.

sources.description: The evidence behind the band, at least one required for a non-null level (build/validate.py). Mostly registry and hub endpoints: Hugging Face downloads, PyPI and npm statistics, OpenRouter token share, GitHub stars where nothing better exists, traffic and MAU trackers for the closed consumer surfaces. Cite the page that SHOWS the current number rather than a homepage. This is the axis where a re-fetch can re-derive the score outright, so a citation resolving to a figure is worth more here than anywhere else.

last_verified.description: The most recent date on which everything in this axis's score was confirmed still correct. Written when the axis is re-checked against its sources, whether or not the value changed. Absent means never confirmed, in which case freshness falls back to the score file's last commit date. Never backfill it from source access dates: opening a URL is a weaker claim than re-confirming a conclusion, and no aggregation of accessed dates fixes that. Normative definition in docs/reference/evidence-and-freshness.md.

capability.description: How good the product is at what it does. The same shape once more: `score` is the graded judgment, `basis` with `basis_detail` is the instrument (adoption's `signal_type`), and `relative_to` with `relation` are the recorded inputs (openness's `components`). Two differences matter. No rubric declares a capability ladder, so nothing derives the score from what is recorded; and the bands are comparable within a category only, never across one. What places many bands is a comparison to a peer, which is why the recorded-inputs slot here is a pair of pointers rather than an evidence string. docs/reference/evidence-and-freshness.md, 'What a capability confirmation attests to', is normative on what a date on this axis does and does not claim.

score.description: The graded capability band, 1-5, comparable within a category and never across one, because capability means different things for a model, a training framework and a dataset. Null where the axis does not apply - 26 products, datasets and a wire protocol among them - which is an abstention rather than a gap. Non-null needs at least one source (build/validate.py). Unlike openness nothing computes it: no rubric declares a capability formula, and measured 2026-08-08, 322 of 472 products record `basis: feature_matrix` against 86 `benchmark`. Read by build/check_capability.py, which requires a recorded `relation` to be arithmetically consistent with this score and the peer's, and by build/serialize.py, which blends it with adoption.level into the product overall score the category stage ladder reads (docs/reference/gap-analysis.md).

basis.description: Which INSTRUMENT the band was read with, not what it measured. Four, because these are four genuinely different things and a checker that cannot tell them apart cannot route or gate the axis: `benchmark` is a published number, `training_value` is ablation or downstream-model evidence, `feature_matrix` is a judgment over what the product does, `n/a` is an honest abstention. This was 85 free-text strings until 2026-08-08, 65 of them used once, with the benchmark's NAME jammed into the string in 56 spellings; that detail now lives in `basis_detail`.

value.description: The reading the band was taken from, quoted rather than interpreted: the benchmark figure, the arena placement, or the sentence of coverage a feature judgment rests on. `basis_detail` names the instrument, this carries what it said. Typed to allow a number and in practice never one - measured 2026-08-08, 373 of 472 are prose strings and 99 are null, not a single bare figure. That is the concrete reason capability has no ladder: there is nothing tokenized here for a formula to read, at 61% prose by check_rubric's measure against the 71% that stopped edge_hardware. Nothing computes on it; it is the `Value` row in the product detail panel.

confidence.description: How sure the curator was of the band. Same scale and the same absence of readers as the other two axes; measured 2026-08-08, high on 219, medium on 229 and low on 24 of 472. Note what it does not encode: a `high` here can sit on a feature-matrix judgment with no measurement under it at all, because this is the curator's certainty rather than the strength of the instrument. `basis` is the field that names the instrument.

note.description: The prose behind the band: what the product does well, what it sits a step below, and against whom. Hand-written and parsed by nothing. This is where the axis's real instrument lived until 2026-08-08: roughly a hundred notes place the band against a named peer in the same category ('one tier below the Megatron-LM anchor'), and in `finetuning_code` every one of the 27 notes does it. `relative_to` and `relation` now record that comparison as data, on 27 products as of 2026-08-08, and `build/check_capability.py --candidates` reports the notes that look like they should carry it. Rendered as `Detail` in the product detail panel.

sources.description: The evidence behind the band, at least one required for a non-null score (build/validate.py). Leaderboards and papers where a benchmark exists - Artificial Analysis, LMArena, Epoch AI, the Open LLM Leaderboard lineage, domain benchmarks such as ANN-Benchmarks - and documentation or feature pages where none does. Weaker than the other two axes' evidence by construction: the peer comparison that places many bands has no cited source of its own, so a capability source usually corroborates the band rather than establishing it.

last_verified.description: The most recent date on which everything in this axis's score was confirmed still correct. Written when the axis is re-checked against its sources, whether or not the value changed. Absent means never confirmed, in which case freshness falls back to the score file's last commit date. Never backfill it from source access dates: opening a URL is a weaker claim than re-confirming a conclusion, and no aggregation of accessed dates fixes that. Normative definition in docs/reference/evidence-and-freshness.md.

basis_detail.description: What the instrument was, in prose: the benchmark's name for `benchmark`, the kind of coverage for `feature_matrix`, `superseded` or `ablation` for `training_value`. Free text on purpose - the enum is what a checker reads, and this is what a reader needs. Not yet controlled; the benchmark names in particular are a normalization job of their own.

relative_to.description: The slug of the product THIS band was placed against, when it was placed by comparison rather than measured. Peer-relative placement is a major capability instrument - the note usually says something like 'one tier below the Megatron-LM anchor' - and until this field existed that comparison lived in an English sentence where nothing could check it, refresh it, or notice when it went stale. Recording it makes the claim falsifiable: build/check_capability.py requires the relation to be arithmetically consistent with both recorded scores, and requires the target's confirmation to be at least as recent as this one's. Same category as this product. Normative definition in docs/reference/evidence-and-freshness.md. Declared on capability only, and `additionalProperties: false` on all three axes keeps it there: a `relation` written onto openness or adoption used to validate silently and be read by nothing, which a sweep run produced on four axes before this was closed.

relation.description: How this product's band sits against `relative_to`. Required with it, and meaningless without it. Deliberately tiny and domain-free, so it generalizes across categories as different as edge_hardware and benchmark_eval_data without asserting anything about what capability means in either.

source.description: One citation: a URL, what it showed, and when it was read. The same shape on all three axes, so a reader who can audit an openness source can audit an adoption one. The first three fields are required and are the audit trail itself; `establishes`, `http_status` and `content_sha256` are the machinery the 2026-07/08 verification work added to make a claimed confirmation checkable, and are forward-populated rather than backfilled - 45 sources carry `establishes` and 73 carry a digest, of 1,857 (2026-08-08).

url.description: The URL that was fetched, http(s) only. Bottom link of the audit chain: score <- the rule that fired <- openness.components <- sources[].shows <- this (docs/reference/evidence-and-freshness.md). Cite the page that actually shows the claim, and prefer the endpoint a re-fetch can reproduce, an API response over a page whose numbers are injected client-side. Measured 2026-08-08 there are 1,131 distinct URLs behind 1,857 citations, which is why the re-read surface is about 1,100 fetches rather than 1,370 axes. build/fetch_source.py fetches it the way build/check_refetch.py will re-fetch it, deliberately through the same call so that a digest mismatch means drift rather than a different client; check_refetch fails on one digest recorded against two different URLs, which has no innocent reading.

shows.description: What THIS source specifically demonstrates, quoted from the body that was fetched. Its whole job is letting somebody else check the work without trusting the curator, so a good one is an extract that could only have come from that page: '`gated: false`, `private: false`, card license `odc-by`', 'MIT License text', '13,834 monthly downloads'. A bad one asserts nothing and would fit any URL in the corpus: 'flagship phase-C verification source' is on 136 of the 1,857 entries as of 2026-08-08. sources/evidence_policy.yaml declares that phrase boilerplate and build/serialize_rubric.py rejects those rows into the warehouse's product_score_sources carrying their reason, so an unsourced assertion becomes a queryable work list instead of passing for provenance. There is deliberately no minimum-length rule: a 25-character floor would throw out 'MIT License text' and keep every filler row, because length measures verbosity, not specificity. Free prose and staying that way - 1,684 distinct strings across 1,857 entries, with 458 of the 1,131 URLs cited more than once and described afresh each time. Write it from the body build/fetch_source.py saved with --body-dir, so the extract comes from what was served rather than from memory.

accessed.description: The date this URL was fetched, ISO 8601. The only field here that dates an observation of something OUTSIDE the repo, which is why the verification invariant is written over it: `last_verified: D` holds only if, for every dimension the score records, some source that `establishes` that dimension was accessed on or after D. It is never aggregated INTO `last_verified`, neither the min (#108) nor the max (#115); both shipped, put a derived date on 19 of the 26 axes then carrying one, and were reverted. docs/reference/evidence-and-freshness.md and docs/reference/evidence-and-freshness.md are normative. Typed as a non-empty string because the corpus quotes the date in YAML, but build/validate.py parses it as an ISO date and rejects a future one - apply_scores refuses to move a stored date backwards, so a future date once written would be protected indefinitely by the guard meant to preserve real checks. One date per source rather than per axis, written by whoever performed the fetch: measured 2026-08-08, 995 of 1,857 carry 2026-06-04, the initial pass.

establishes.description: Which dimensions of this axis's score THIS source settles. `sources` is a flat list per axis, so without it nothing records which source establishes which dimension, and a re-check claim cannot be checked. Every name must be a dimension some category's scoring_recipe declares, or a recorded key one of those dimensions reads; build/validate.py enforces that cross-file, because a typo'd name would establish nothing while looking like attribution. Optional and forward-populated: build/check_verification.py requires it only on axes that claim a last_verified. Normative definition in docs/reference/evidence-and-freshness.md.

http_status.description: HTTP status the fetch at `accessed` returned. Present means something actually made a request. A 404 at re-check time says the URL was either never real or has rotted.

content_sha256.description: SHA-256 of the fetched response body at `accessed` time. A changed digest says the page moved under a claim that still cites it — a reason to re-check rather than a failure on its own, since pages legitimately change. A MISSING digest on a newly claimed confirmation is a hard failure, because it means the tool fetched nothing.
